title: The search that skips past what it was looking for

prereqs.why: The broken loop is a correct binary search for a different question; telling the two apart is the exercise.
The invariant on the two halves is what says which side an element equal to x belongs on.
The search takes &[i64], and the empty-slice case is a boundary the loop has to survive.

statement:
**This one is already written, and it is wrong.** Your job is to find out why and fix it.

`lower_bound(v, x)` answers: **what is the index of the first element of `v` that is not less than `x`?** The slice is sorted and may contain repeats. If every element is smaller than `x`, the answer is `v.len()` — one past the end, which is where `x` would be inserted.

```
n                 0 <= n <= 100000
v[0] .. v[n-1]    sorted, non-decreasing, each fits in i64
q                 number of queries
x  (q of them)    one per line
```

Print one index per query, one per line.

### The failing sample

```
v = [10, 20, 20, 30]

  x = 5   -> 0    nothing is smaller than 5
  x = 20  -> 1    the FIRST 20 is at index 1
  x = 25  -> 3    the first element not less than 25 is the 30
  x = 99  -> 4    everything is smaller; one past the end
```

The code in the editor gets two of those four right. It answers `3` for `x = 20`, and it answers `1` for `x = 10`. Absent values are fine; it is **values that are actually in the slice** that come back wrong, and the error is exactly the number of times the value appears.

### What is being asked

Any implementation meeting the specification passes — a hand-written loop, `partition_point`, anything. You are not reproducing a particular patch. The exercise is to say precisely which question the loop is answering, and why that is not the question that was asked.

The hidden tests include an empty slice, a slice that is all one value, queries below and above everything, and a hundred thousand elements — so a linear scan will be too slow.
hints: Run it. Two of the four sample queries are right. Write down, for a value that IS present, what the code returns and what it should return: the gap is the number of copies of that value. A search that lands just after a run of equal values is not broken by accident — it is answering a different, equally reasonable question.

There are two standard answers for a sorted slice: the first index where `x` could be inserted keeping order (`lower_bound`), and the last such index (`upper_bound`). They differ only on values that are present, and by exactly the number of copies. The loop in the editor is a correct implementation — of the other one.

Look at the comparison inside the loop. The invariant you want is that everything below `lo` is `< x` and everything from `hi` up is `>= x`. When `v[mid]` is **equal** to `x`, which side of that line is it on? The code moves `lo` past it, which is the rule for `>` rather than for `>=`.
